title: Spiny Amaranth: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Spiny Amaranth in Rice: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Spiny amaranth, or kulitis, hides sharp spines and can make 117,000 seeds per plant. Learn to spot it and clear it from your rice field safely.
excerpt: Spiny amaranth is a broadleaf weed with sharp spines that grows in rainfed lowland rice fields across the Philippines. One plant can make a huge amount of seed, and it also hosts a nematode that harms rice roots. This page shows how to spot it, why it matters to your palay, and how to remove it safely.

blocks.text:
This damo belongs to the amaranth family, and farmers know it by many local names. Depending on the region, people call it alayon, ayang lalaki, ayantoto, baoan, bayambang, harum, gitingiting, kalitis, kalunai, kuanton, kudiapa, kulitis, taikada or uray. Spiny amaranth grows in rainfed lowland rice fields, where the soil stays dry for part of the season.

As an annual, it lives through one season and then dies. But it leaves plenty behind, because it spreads by seed and one plant can drop more than a hundred thousand of them. The seeds come tiny, round and shiny black, so you hardly notice them on the soil. They wait there until the field dries out enough for them to sprout.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about spiny amaranth
rows: Alayon, ayang lalaki, ayantoto, baoan, bayambang, harum, gitingiting, kalitis, kalunai, kuanton, kudiapa, kulitis, taikada, uray

blocks.text: Run your eye along the stem before you touch it. This weed has branched, pale green stems with a pair of thin, sharp spines where each leaf and branch joins the stem. The leaves grow one at a time, oval to broadly lance shaped, and narrow down into a leaf stalk at the base. As a broadleaf weed, it has wide leaves with netted veins. At the tips and in the leaf angles, look for packed spikes of small green flowers.

items: Pairs of thin, sharp spines where the leaves and branches meet the stem.
Pale green, branched stems that prick your hands when you grab them carelessly.
Simple oval to broadly lance shaped leaves, set one at a time along the stem.
Leaf blades that narrow down into a clear leaf stalk at the base.
Dense spikes and clusters of tiny green flowers at the tips and leaf angles.
Look alike tip: slender amaranth looks similar but has no spines, so check the leaf joints.

blocks.text:
Spiny amaranth is a C4 weed. That means it uses strong sun and heat very well, so it can grow fast in open, dry patches of the field. Each plant can produce 117,000 seeds, which is why a few plants today can turn into a thick stand next season. So far, researchers have not reported how strongly it competes with rice for yield.

The bigger hidden danger lies underground. This weed serves as an alternative host of Meloidogyne graminicola, the rice root knot nematode. These tiny worms cause galls, or swellings, on rice roots. When this weed grows in or around the field, the nematodes can live on it even while no rice stands in the paddy.

items: Always wear thick gloves when you pull it. Grip the stem low, below the spines, and pull out the whole root.
Remove plants before the flower spikes ripen. One plant can drop 117,000 seeds, so even a few missed plants restock the soil.
Clear it from levees and fallow fields too, since it can keep the rice root knot nematode alive between crops.
Do not leave pulled plants with ripe spikes on the levee. Pile them away from the field where seeds cannot fall back into the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold spiny amaranth down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Spiny Amaranth Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Spiny Amaranth?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Spiny Amaranth

items.q: What is spiny amaranth called in Tagalog?
items.a: Many Tagalog speaking farmers call it kulitis or uray. In other regions you may hear alayon, ayang lalaki, kalitis, kudiapa or bayambang, among others. Some of these names also cover slender amaranth, so check the stem before you decide. If you see pairs of sharp spines where the leaves join the stem, you have the spiny kind.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Start with prevention: use clean seed and keep the levees free of weeds. Keep standing water in the field where you can, since amaranth seeds sprout poorly under flood. Then hand weed with gloves while plants are small, before the spikes ripen. If you need a herbicide, pick one made for broadleaf weeds that suits the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is this weed harmful to rice besides the spines?
items.a: Yes. Its seeds come first, since one plant can produce 117,000 of them. It also shelters Meloidogyne graminicola, a nematode that forms galls on rice roots. Galled roots take up less water and food, so the palay grows weak. Even so, researchers have not yet reported how much yield it takes through direct competition with rice.
